snippet: Knock it out of the park with our new planner.
why: Baseball idiom; baseball is barely known in Russia, so the image means nothing and a literal translation sounds odd.

snippet: We're nuts about almonds.
why: Nuts pun (crazy + nuts) can't be kept in Russian; needs a new joke or plain copy.

snippet: Mother's Day is May 10. Order her gift now!
why: Russia celebrates Mother's Day on the last Sunday of November, not in May.

snippet: Merry Christmas! Free delivery on December 25.
why: Orthodox Christmas is January 7; New Year is the main gift holiday, so Dec 25 is the wrong hook.

snippet: Score a touchdown with these savings.
why: American football is not widely followed; the metaphor won't land.

snippet: Surprise her with a dozen red roses.
why: An even number of flowers is for funerals in Russia; gifts use odd numbers.

snippet: Whistle while you work. Our new office playlist is here.
why: Whistling indoors is believed to bring money loss; an odd thing to encourage at work.

snippet: Hey buddy, your order's here!
why: Forces a ты/вы choice; overly familiar tone can feel disrespectful for many brands.

snippet: Our new budgeting app is a piece of cake.
why: Piece of cake means nothing literally in Russian; needs a local equivalent like "проще простого".

snippet: Don't miss the boat: the sale ends Friday.
why: Nautical idiom has no Russian equivalent; a literal translation reads as nonsense.

snippet: Lettuce celebrate! 20% off all salads.
why: Lettuce/let us pun only works in English; needs new wordplay or plain copy.

snippet: Our cheese deals are un-brie-lievable.
why: Brie pun can't survive translation; the joke disappears.

snippet: Give thanks with our Thanksgiving dinner bundle.
why: Thanksgiving isn't celebrated in Russia; the whole campaign hook is irrelevant.

snippet: Hit a home run with your next presentation.
why: Baseball metaphor; unfamiliar to most Russian readers.

snippet: It's the Super Bowl of sales!
why: US-specific sports event; little cultural weight in Russia.

snippet: Brighten her day with a bouquet of yellow flowers.
why: Yellow flowers are traditionally associated with separation; risky for a romantic gift message.

snippet: Pack a PB&J for the road. Our lunchboxes keep it fresh!
why: Peanut butter and jelly sandwiches aren't a common Russian staple; the everyday image doesn't resonate and "PB&J" is unknown.

snippet: Spring break is coming! Book your beach getaway now.
why: Spring break is a US college tradition with no Russian equivalent; school holidays in Russia run on a different calendar and aren't tied to beach trips.

snippet: You go, girl! Crush your goals.
why: Slangy cheerleading tone has no natural equivalent; sounds forced or patronizing in Russian.

snippet: Smile! Our staff greet every guest with a big smile.
why: Constant smiling at strangers can read as insincere in Russian culture; depends on brand and context.

snippet: Your order has shipped and will arrive in 3–5 business days.
why: Neutral transactional text; nothing culturally specific.

snippet: Reset your password using the link below.
why: Standard account message; translates directly.

snippet: Your subscription renews automatically each month.
why: Plain billing information; no cultural reference.

snippet: Thank you for your feedback. Our team will review it shortly.
why: Polite, neutral customer service text.

snippet: New features are now available. Update the app to try them.
why: Neutral product update; no idioms or references.

snippet: Your profile is 80% complete. Add a photo to finish.
why: Simple progress message; nothing market-specific.

snippet: We couldn't process your payment. Please check your card details.
why: Clear error message; neutral tone.

snippet: Save your favorite items to view them later.
why: Basic feature description; translates directly.

snippet: Your account settings have been updated.
why: Confirmation message; nothing to adapt.

snippet: Need help? Contact our support team any time.
why: Standard support line; neutral and universal.

snippet: Assume nothing.
why: DOCUMENTED: HSBC slogan reported to render as "Do nothing" in several markets; HSBC replaced it in its 2009 rebrand.

snippet: Pajero
why: DOCUMENTED: Mitsubishi Pajero; "pajero" is vulgar slang in Spanish, so the model was sold as "Montero" there.

snippet: Fitta
why: DOCUMENTED: Honda's planned name for the Jazz/Fit; vulgar slang in Nordic languages, renamed before launch.

snippet: Coca-Cola
why: PARTLY TRUE: shopkeepers' phonetic signs reportedly read like "bite the wax tadpole"; the company itself chose 可口可乐 ("delicious happiness").

snippet: Finger-lickin' good.
why: DISPUTED: KFC slogan said to have come out as "eat your fingers off" in China; widely repeated, sourcing is thin.

snippet: Turn it loose.
why: DISPUTED: Coors slogan said to read as "suffer from diarrhea" in Spanish; commonly cited, weak sourcing.

snippet: It won't leak in your pocket and embarrass you.
why: DISPUTED: Parker Pen story; "embarazar" means "to make pregnant", not "embarrass". Likely apocryphal but the false friend is real.

snippet: Come alive with the Pepsi Generation.
why: DISPUTED: said to have become "Pepsi brings your ancestors back from the grave"; probably a legend.

snippet: Benz
why: DISPUTED: early transliteration "Bensi" reportedly sounded like "rush to die"; brand uses 奔驰 (Benchi) today.

snippet: Nova
why: MYTH: the Chevy Nova "no va" ("doesn't go") story is false; "nova" and "no va" read differently and the car sold well in Latin America.
